title: 04. Caching: LRU (Least Recently Used)
summary: LRU is a cache eviction policy that evicts the entry that was accessed least recently, based on the heuristic that "if you haven't used it lately, you won't use it soon." Implemented with a hashmap plus a doubly-linked list,…
objectives: What is LRU, and how does it achieve O(1) per operation?
Why does LRU use a doubly-linked list instead of a singly-linked list or an array?
What is scan pollution, and why is LRU vulnerable to it?
What is Segmented LRU, and how does it improve scan resistance?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** LRU is a cache eviction policy that **evicts the entry that was accessed least recently**, based on the heuristic that "if you haven't used it lately, you won't use it soon." Implemented with a hashmap plus a doubly-linked list, LRU achieves **O(1) per access** and adapts quickly to access-pattern shifts, at the cost of poor scan resistance.

LRU is the most widely-deployed eviction policy because it is simple, fast, and good enough for most workloads. The intuition is **temporal locality**: keys accessed recently are likely to be re-accessed soon (a user viewing product A is likely to view it again, or view related products in the same session). LRU maintains a strict ordering of cache entries by recency — the most recently accessed entry is at the head, the least recently accessed at the tail — and on eviction, removes the tail. The data structure that supports O(1) updates is a **hashmap plus doubly-linked list**: the hashmap maps each key to its linked-list node (O(1) lookup), and the doubly-linked list supports O(1) removal and re-insertion (move a node to the head on access, remove the tail on eviction). Real-world: Redis's `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` (an approximate LRU using sampling), Memcached's LRU (with a segmented design since 1.4.x), Linux kernel's page cache reclaim (an LRU-variant with active/inactive lists), and Python's `functools.lru_cache` decorator (which uses an `OrderedDict` internally).

The **operations** are: (1) **Get(key)**: look up the key in the hashmap. If present, move the node to the head of the list (mark as most recently used) and return the value — O(1). If absent, return a miss. (2) **Put(key, value)**: if the key exists, update the value and move the node to the head — O(1). If new, create a node at the head; if the cache is full, evict the tail first (remove from list and hashmap) — O(1). (3) **Eviction**: the tail of the list is the least recently used entry; remove it and delete from the hashmap — O(1). All operations are O(1) because the hashmap gives O(1) lookup and the doubly-linked list gives O(1) update given the node pointer. The space overhead is two pointers per entry (prev, next) plus the hashmap entry — typically 16–24 bytes per cached entry, modest compared to the value size.

The **scan-resistance weakness** is LRU's defining flaw. When a sequential scan reads N cold keys (e.g., a backup job reading every key once), each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys, so the scan evicts up to N hot keys — even though the scanned keys will never be re-accessed. After the scan, the cache is full of cold data, and the next access to a hot key misses. Example: a 1000-entry cache with a 100-key hot working set at 95% hit rate; a backup scans 5000 cold keys; the cache ends up with the last 1000 scanned keys (all cold) and 0 hot keys; hit rate drops to 0% until the hot keys are re-accessed and re-loaded. The "working set" is effectively wiped. Real-world: a Redis cache with `allkeys-lru` will see hit rate collapse during backups, crawls, or analytics scans — operators must use `allkeys-lfu` or W-TinyLFU if scans are common.

The **variants** address LRU's weaknesses. **Segmented LRU** (used by Caffeine, Memcached) divides the cache into a "probationary" segment (new admissions) and a "protected" segment (entries accessed multiple times); a second access promotes an entry from probationary to protected, and only probationary entries are evicted first. This gives some scan resistance — a one-time scan populates probationary, but the protected hot set stays resident. **LRU-K** (K-step LRU) tracks the time of the K-th most recent access; eviction considers the K-th access time, not the most recent, so a single scan access doesn't immediately promote a key — the key must be accessed K times to "count." **2Q** (Two Queues) is similar: new entries go to an "AmiQueue" (probationary); on second access, they move to the main LRU. **ARC** (Adaptive Replacement Cache) combines LRU and LFU adaptively. All these variants trade some implementation complexity for better scan resistance; the simplest scan-resistant improvement is the segmented design.

The **concurrency** challenges of LRU are significant. The doubly-linked list is a shared mutable structure — every access moves a node to the head, which requires updating multiple pointers under a lock. In a single-threaded cache (Python's `functools.lru_cache`), this is fine. In a multi-threaded cache, the lock becomes a bottleneck at high throughput. Solutions: (1) **Segmented LRU with per-segment locks** — divide keys across N segments (by hash), each with its own LRU list and lock; concurrent accesses to different segments don't contend. (2) **Approximate LRU** (Redis's approach) — don't maintain a global list; on eviction, sample N random keys and pick the least recently used among the sample; this avoids the lock contention at the cost of ~5% hit-rate loss. (3) **Lock-free LRU** — use CAS (compare-and-swap) operations on the linked list; complex but extremely high throughput. Caffeine uses a non-blocking design with a windowed TinyLFU admission; it's effectively lock-free for most operations. Real-world: Redis's `maxmemory-samples` controls the sample size (default 5); bumping to 10 gets closer to true LRU at higher CPU cost.

The **comparison with LFU** is the key design decision. LRU wins when the hot set shifts (LRU adapts within a few cache-misses; LFU adapts slowly because old counts persist). LRU loses to LFU on scan-heavy workloads (LRU is demolished by scans; LFU is scan-resistant). LRU loses to LFU on stable-hot-set workloads (LFU's frequency tracking gives a stronger signal than LRU's recency). The modern consensus is to use **W-TinyLFU** (which combines recency and frequency) when implementation complexity is acceptable, or **LRU** as a safe default when complexity must be minimized. Real-world: Redis recommends `allkeys-lru` for general workloads and `allkeys-lfu` for stable hot keys; Caffeine defaults to W-TinyLFU; Memcached uses LRU with a segmented design for scan resistance.

A subtle but important point: **LRU's O(1) is amortized, not worst-case**, in some implementations. In a concurrent LRU with lazy deletion (mark nodes as deleted, clean up later), individual operations are O(1) but a periodic cleanup is O(n). In an LRU with hash rebalancing (when the hashmap grows), the resize is O(n) but amortized O(1) per operation. These amortized costs are usually acceptable, but they can cause tail latency spikes — a 1 ms operation that occasionally takes 10 ms (during cleanup or resize) is bad for latency-sensitive workloads. Real-world: Redis's approximate LRU avoids these spikes by design (no global list, no cleanup); Caffeine's lock-free design also avoids spikes. For latency-sensitive caches, prefer implementations with bounded worst-case per operation.

The **decision to use LRU** often comes down to: (1) Is the workload scan-free or scan-light? (2) Is implementation simplicity important? (3) Is the hot set stable or shifting? For scan-free workloads with shifting hot sets (typical session caches, recently-viewed lists), LRU is the right default. For scan-heavy workloads (catalogs with periodic crawls), LFU or W-TinyLFU is better. For stable hot sets (popular products, trending videos), LFU's frequency signal gives a slightly higher hit rate. For mixed workloads (real-world), W-TinyLFU dominates. Real-world: Python's `functools.lru_cache` uses LRU because it's simple and good enough for in-process caching; Redis's default `maxmemory-policy` is `noeviction` but operators typically switch to `allkeys-lru` for general workloads.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Get[Get key] --> Lookup{In hashmap?}
    Lookup -->|Yes| Hit[Move node to HEAD]
    Lookup -->|No| Miss[Return miss]
    Hit --> Return[Return value]

    Put[Put key, value] --> Exists{Key exists?}
    Exists -->|Yes| Update[Update value, move to HEAD]
    Exists -->|No| Full{Cache full?}
    Full -->|Yes| Evict[Evict TAIL node, remove from hashmap]
    Full -->|No| Insert[Insert new node at HEAD, add to hashmap]
    Evict --> Insert

    subgraph LRUTable[LRU Doubly-Linked List + Hashmap]
        H[HEAD: most recent] --> N1[Node1] --> N2[Node2] --> N3[Node3] --> T[TAIL: least recent]
        HM[Hashmap: key -> node pointer]
    end
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
LRU = Hashmap (O(1) lookup) + Doubly-Linked List (O(1) reorder)

Hashmap:                Doubly-Linked List (recency order):
  +-------------+         +------+    +------+    +------+
  | key "A"     |         | HEAD |--->|nodeA |--->|nodeB |
  | -> nodeA    |         +------+    +------+    +------+
  +-------------+              |          ^          |
                               v          |          v
  +-------------+         +------+    +------+    +------+
  | key "B"     |         |nodeB |<---|nodeA |<---| HEAD |
  | -> nodeB    |         +------+    +------+    +------+
  +-------------+
                         (most recent)         (least recent)
  +-------------+         +------+    +------+    +------+
  | key "C"     |         |nodeA |<-> |nodeB |<-> |nodeC |--> TAIL
  | -> nodeC    |         +------+    +------+    +------+
  +-------------+

GET("A"):  (cache hit)
  1. hashmap["A"] --> nodeA         (O(1) lookup)
  2. move nodeA to HEAD             (O(1) pointer update)
  3. return valueA

PUT("D", valD):  (cache full, must evict)
  1. evict TAIL (nodeC)             (O(1) remove from list + hashmap)
  2. insert nodeD at HEAD           (O(1) pointer update)
  3. hashmap["D"] --> nodeD

Result:  +---+   +---+   +---+
         | D |-->| A |-->| B |   (C evicted as least recently used)
         +---+   +---+   +---+

Scan-resistance weakness:
  Before scan:
  +----+   +----+   +----+          +----+
  | H1 |-->| H2 |-->...-->| H100 |  |TAIL|  (hot set resident, 95% hit)
  +----+   +----+   +----+          +----+

  Scan of 100 cold keys (C1..C100):
  Each Ci inserted at HEAD, pushes hot toward TAIL.

  After scan:
  +-----+   +-----+          +-----+
  |C100 |-->| C99 |-->...-->| C1  |-->TAIL  (hot set EVICTED)
  +-----+   +-----+          +-----+

  Next access to H1 --> MISS (cache polluted by scan)
```

### Walkthrough
1. **Get on hit**: The hashmap lookup returns the node pointer in O(1). The node is moved to the head of the doubly-linked list (marking it most recently used) by updating four pointers (prev/next on the node and its neighbors) — O(1). The value is returned.
2. **Put on full cache**: A new key arrives but the cache is at capacity. The tail node (least recently used) is removed from the list and the hashmap — O(1). The new node is inserted at the head and added to the hashmap — O(1). The evicted entry's memory is freed.
3. **Scan pollution**: A long sequential read of cold keys evicts the hot working set. Each scanned key is inserted at the head, pushing the previous head toward the tail; after N scans (where N >= cache size), the entire cache is cold data, and the hot keys are gone. This is LRU's main weakness, motivating LFU and W-TinyLFU.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- LRU cache using collections.OrderedDict.
- A node in the doubly-linked list.
- Hand-rolled LRU: hashmap for lookup, doubly-linked list for recency.
- Remove a node from the linked list (O(1)).
- LRU Cache: two implementations.
- 1. Simple: OrderedDict-based (Python standard library).
- 2. Hand-rolled: hashmap + doubly-linked list (textbook O(1) version).
- Implementation 1: OrderedDict (simple, idiomatic)

**Defines:** `LRUCacheOrderedDict`, `_Node`, `LRUCacheLinkedList`, `demo()`

```python
# LRU Cache: two implementations.
# 1. Simple: OrderedDict-based (Python standard library).
# 2. Hand-rolled: hashmap + doubly-linked list (textbook O(1) version).

from collections import OrderedDict
from typing import Any, Optional

# ---------- Implementation 1: OrderedDict (simple, idiomatic) ---------- #
class LRUCacheOrderedDict:
    """LRU cache using collections.OrderedDict.

    OrderedDict.move_to_end(key) marks the key as most recently used.
    OrderedDict.popitem(last=False) evicts the oldest (FIFO end) key.
    Both operations are O(1).
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.store: OrderedDict = OrderedDict()
        self.stats = {"hits": 0, "misses": 0, "evictions": 0}

    def get(self, key: Any) -> Optional[Any]:
        if key in self.store:
            self.store.move_to_end(key)  # mark as recently used
            self.stats["hits"] += 1
            return self.store[key]
        self.stats["misses"] += 1
        return None

    def put(self, key: Any, value: Any) -> None:
        if key in self.store:
            self.store.move_to_end(key)
            self.store[key] = value
            return
        if len(self.store) >= self.cap:
            self.store.popitem(last=False)  # evict oldest
            self.stats["evictions"] += 1
        self.store[key] = value

# ---------- Implementation 2: Hashmap + Doubly-Linked List ---------- #
class _Node:
    """A node in the doubly-linked list."""
    __slots__ = ("key", "value", "prev", "next")

    def __init__(self, key=None, value=None):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

class LRUCacheLinkedList:
    """Hand-rolled LRU: hashmap for lookup, doubly-linked list for recency.

    All operations (get, put, evict) are O(1).
    Sentinel head/tail nodes simplify boundary conditions.
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.hashmap: dict = {}  # key -> _Node
        # Sentinel nodes: head.next is most recent; tail.prev is least recent.
        self.head = _Node()  # sentinel
        self.tail = _Node()  # sentinel
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head
        self.stats = {"hits": 0, "misses": 0, "evictions": 0}

    def _remove(self, node: _Node) -> None:
        """Remove a node from the linked list (O(1))."""
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _add_to_head(self, node: _Node) -> None:
        """Insert a node right after head (most recent position, O(1))."""
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def _move_to_head(self, node: _Node) -> None:
        """Move an existing node to the head (most recent, O(1))."""
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_to_head(node)

    def _evict_tail(self) -> None:
        """Evict the least recently used node (tail.prev)."""
        lru = self.tail.prev
        if lru is self.head:
            return  # empty cache
        self._remove(lru)
        del self.hashmap[lru.key]
        self.stats["evictions"] += 1

    def get(self, key: Any) -> Optional[Any]:
        if key in self.hashmap:
            node = self.hashmap[key]
            self._move_to_head(node)  # mark as recently used
            self.stats["hits"] += 1
            return node.value
        self.stats["misses"] += 1
        return None

    def put(self, key: Any, value: Any) -> None:
        if key in self.hashmap:
            node = self.hashmap[key]
            node.value = value
            self._move_to_head(node)
            return
        if len(self.hashmap) >= self.cap:
            self._evict_tail()
        node = _Node(key=key, value=value)
        self.hashmap[key] = node
        self._add_to_head(node)

# ---------- Demo ---------- #
def demo(cache, name):
    print(f"--- {name} (capacity=3) ---")
    cache.put("A", 1)
    cache.put("B", 2)
    cache.put("C", 3)
    print(f"  get('A')={cache.get('A')}  (hit, A moved to head)")
    print(f"  get('B')={cache.get('B')}  (hit, B moved to head)")
    cache.put("D", 4)  # cache full, C is LRU -> evict C
    print(f"  put('D',4) -> evicts C (least recently used)")
    print(f"  get('C')={cache.get('C')}  (miss, C was evicted)")
    print(f"  get('D')={cache.get('D')}  (hit)")
    print(f"  get('A')={cache.get('A')}  (hit, A still resident)")
    print(f"  stats: {cache.stats}")
    print()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo(LRUCacheOrderedDict(3), "OrderedDict-based LRU")
    demo(LRUCacheLinkedList(3), "Hashmap + LinkedList LRU")

    # ---- Scan-resistance demo ----
    print("--- Scan-resistance demo (capacity=100) ---")
    cache = LRUCacheLinkedList(100)
    # Hot set: 100 keys, each put 10x (fills the cache).
    for _ in range(10):
        for k in range(1, 101):
            cache.put(k, f"v{k}")
    print(f"  After hot-set warmup: size={len(cache.hashmap)} (cache full)")

    # Scan: 100 cold keys via put. Each insert evicts the LRU hot key.
    for k in range(1001, 1101):
        cache.put(k, f"v{k}")
    print(f"  After scan of 100 cold keys (put): "
          f"evictions={cache.stats['evictions']}")

    # Now request a hot key — should miss (evicted by the scan).
    hot_val = cache.get(1)
    print(f"  get(hot key 1) after scan: {hot_val}  "
          f"(None = evicted by scan pollution)")
    print(f"  >> LRU is NOT scan-resistant — hot set wiped by sequential scan.")
```

quiz.explanation: LRU (Least Recently Used) is a cache eviction policy that removes the entry accessed least recently when the cache is full. The intuition is temporal locality: recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed soon.

options: This is a workload with both temporal locality (recently-watched predicts next-watch) and a stable hot set (popular shows) — both signals are useful.

quiz.explanation: A doubly-linked list is required because LRU needs to remove an arbitrary node (the accessed node, to move it to the head) in O(1) — given only the node pointer (from the hashmap). In a singly-linked list, removing an arbitrary node requires knowing its predecessor, which means walking the list from the head — O(n).

quiz.explanation: Scan pollution occurs when a sequential read of cold keys displaces the hot working set from the cache. LRU is vulnerable because every access (even a one-time scan read) updates recency — each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys, so the scan evicts hot keys to make room. After a scan of N keys (where N >= cache size), the cache holds the last N scanned keys (all cold) and 0 hot keys.

quiz.explanation: Segmented LRU divides the cache into two segments: a probationary segment (new admissions) and a protected segment (entries accessed multiple times). New entries are admitted to the probationary segment; on a second access, they're promoted to the protected segment.
